concepts.title: Measuring Heights Using Parallel Lines
concepts.one_liner: The height of an object can be estimated from a single image by projecting its vertical segment onto a reference object of known height using vanishing points and the cross-ratio invariant.
concepts.content:
To measure the height of an object (e.g., a desk) given a reference object (e.g., a bookshelf) in a scene, we must account for perspective projection which prevents direct comparison of 2D image distances. (see figure: Given the height of a reference object, the location of the horizon line and one vanishing point, how can we estimate the height of other objects in the scene?)

First, we project the desk height onto the bookshelf using the following steps in homogeneous coordinates:
1. Estimate the line $\boldsymbol{l}_1 = \mathbf{g}_d \times \mathbf{g}_b$ passing through the ground points of the desk $\mathbf{g}_d$ and bookshelf $\mathbf{g}_b$.
2. Compute the intersection of $\boldsymbol{l}_1$ with the horizon line $\mathbf{h}$ to find the vanishing point $\mathbf{a} = \boldsymbol{l}_1 \times \mathbf{h}$.
3. Compute the line $\boldsymbol{l}_2 = \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{t}_d$ passing through $\mathbf{a}$ and the top of the desk $\mathbf{t}_d$. Lines $\boldsymbol{l}_1$ and $\boldsymbol{l}_2$ are parallel in 3D and vertically aligned.
4. Find the intersection $\mathbf{b} = \boldsymbol{l}_2 \times (\mathbf{g}_b \times \mathbf{t}_b)$, where $\mathbf{b}$ represents the top of the desk if it were moved into contact with the bookshelf.

The segment between $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{g}_b$ is the projection of the desk height on the bookshelf. Because of perspective foreshortening, we use the cross-ratio invariant between the four collinear points (top of bookshelf $\mathbf{t}_b$, projected desk top $\mathbf{b}$, ground $\mathbf{g}_b$, and vertical vanishing point $\mathbf{v}_3$) to relate image distances to 3D heights:
$$\frac{h_{\text{bookshelf}}}{h_{\text{desk}}} = \frac{\left| \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{v}_3 \right| \left| \mathbf{t}_b - \mathbf{g}_b \right| }{\left| \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{g}_b \right| \left| \mathbf{t}_b - \mathbf{v}_3  \right|}$$
Solving this equality allows for the estimation of the unknown height $h_{\text{desk}}$.
concepts.motivation_md: In single-view metrology, we cannot directly compare the sizes of objects at different depths because perspective projection causes distant objects to appear smaller. This technique solves the problem of measuring an unknown height by geometrically 'moving' it to a reference location where its size can be compared to a known standard using projective invariants.
concepts.recap_md: - Project the target height onto a reference object by finding a common vanishing point on the horizon line.

key_passage.text: Lines $\boldsymbol{l}_1$ and $\boldsymbol{l}_2$ are parallel on 3D and vertically aligned. In order to use the cross-ratio invariant we need two sets of four colinear points related by a projective geometry.

concepts.title: Projective Invariants
concepts.one_liner: Projective invariants are geometric measures that remain unchanged after a perspective projection.
concepts.content: Projective invariants are measures that do not change after perspective projection. The cross-ratio is the most important projective invariant.
concepts.motivation_md: Perspective projection distorts lengths and angles, making it difficult to recover 3D information from 2D images. Projective invariants provide a mathematical way to identify properties that stay constant despite this distortion, enabling 3D reconstruction and measurement.
concepts.recap_md: - Invariants are properties that are preserved under perspective transformations.

key_passage.text: Projective invariants are measures that do not change after perspective projection. The cross-ratio is the most important projective invariant.

concepts.title: Height Propagation to Supported Objects
concepts.one_liner: Height information can be propagated from objects on the ground to objects supported by them to measure heights not in contact with the ground plane.
concepts.content: The method of measuring heights relies on using vertical lines in contact with the ground plane to propagate information from one point in space to another. While this method requires establishing the vertical projection of a point onto a reference plane (like the ground), it can be extended. Once the height of objects in contact with the ground is estimated, that information can be used to propagate 3D measurements to other objects that are not directly on the ground, provided they are supported by objects of known height.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard single-view metrology often requires objects to touch the ground plane to establish a reference. This technique allows for the measurement of 'floating' or stacked objects by treating the supporting object as a secondary reference plane.
concepts.recap_md: - Vertical projection to a reference plane is required to propagate measurements between points.

concepts.title: Supported-by hierarchy
concepts.one_liner: The supported-by hierarchy is the structural parsing of which objects in a scene provide physical support for others.
concepts.content: This procedure highlights the importance of the correct parsing of the supported-by hierarchy between objects in the scene.
concepts.motivation_md: To measure objects not touching the ground, a vision system must understand the physical relationships between objects—specifically, which object supports another—to correctly propagate height measurements upward from the ground plane.

concepts.title: 3D Metrology from a Single View
concepts.one_liner: 3D metrology from a single view uses reference objects and vanishing points to extract 3D locations and measurements from a 2D image.
concepts.content: 3D metrology involves using a reference object to measure other objects and establishing a general framework to locate 3D points. In a typical scene, the axes of a 3D coordinate frame can be aligned with the three dominant orthogonal orientations, which in turn align with the image's vanishing points. (see figure: Can we find out where to put the ticks in the world-coordinate axes as seen by the camera so that they correspond to calibrated measurements? Simply placing them at evenly spaced intervals along the...) By calibrating the projected world-coordinate axes in the image plane, we can transport points into the 3D world axes to measure object sizes and point locations.
concepts.motivation_md: Normally, a single 2D image loses depth information, making 3D measurement impossible. Single-view metrology recovers this information by exploiting geometric constraints like vanishing points and known reference dimensions.
concepts.recap_md: - Vanishing points and reference objects allow for the calibration of 3D axes in a 2D image.

concepts.title: Calibration of the Projected World Axis
concepts.one_liner: Calibrating projected world axes involves using the cross-ratio and reference measurements to place non-linearly spaced tick marks along image axes.
concepts.content: To calibrate world-coordinate axes in an image, one must determine the correct positions for tick marks (e.g., 1m, 2m). Due to perspective distortion, these marks are not evenly spaced in the image plane. The calibration process uses the cross-ratio invariant, the horizon line of a reference plane, the position of orthogonal vanishing points, and the known real-world measurement of at least one object. (see figure: Using the cross-ratio invariant to project the world coordinates into the image using only the vanishing points.) By using reference measurements (such as a bookshelf height or table radius), we can solve for the image locations of specific units (e.g., $\alpha_X=\alpha_Y=\alpha_Z=1$ m). (see figure: Calibrated world axes. Each axis is calibrated using the measurement of a scene element parallel to the world-coordinate axis. In this example, we used the bookshelf height (197 cm) and the radius of...) Once the system is calibrated, one can read 3D information directly, such as the camera height, which corresponds to the horizon line location in a horizontal ground plane scene.
concepts.motivation_md: Because of perspective foreshortening, a pixel distance at the bottom of an image represents a different physical distance than the same pixel distance near the horizon. Calibrating the axes allows us to map these non-linear image coordinates back to linear real-world measurements.
concepts.recap_md: - Perspective distortion prevents even spacing of coordinate ticks in the image plane.

concepts.title: Locating a 3D Point
concepts.one_liner: A 3D point's coordinates can be recovered from a single view by using its projection onto the ground plane and its relationship to calibrated world axes.
concepts.content:
While a single point $\mathbf{P}$ cannot be localized in 3D from a single view without context, the presence of objects and known geometry allows for 3D estimation. If a point $\mathbf{P}$ belongs to an object in contact with the ground, we can identify its ground projection $\mathbf{G}$. (see figure: Figure (a) In the absence of any other information, we can not recover the 3D location of point $\mathbf{P}$. (b) If we are given a way to project the point P into the ground, then we can read out...)

Once $\mathbf{G}$ is located, it can be projected onto the world-coordinate axes. To find the $Y$-coordinate, we find the line $\boldsymbol{l}_3$ through $\mathbf{G}$ and the origin, find its intersection $\mathbf{v}$ with the horizon, and then find the intersection of line $\boldsymbol{l}_4$ (connecting $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{P}$) with the $Y_w$-axis. The $P_x$ and $P_z$ coordinates are found by connecting $\mathbf{G}$ to the vanishing points $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$.
concepts.motivation_md: Recovering 3D coordinates from a 2D image is an ill-posed problem because many 3D points project to the same 2D pixel. By assuming the point is part of an object on a known plane (like the ground), we can resolve this ambiguity.
concepts.recap_md: - Projecting a point onto the ground plane is the key step to resolving its 3D position.

key_passage.text: It suffices to know that the point P belongs to an object that is in contact with the ground and the geometry of this object provides the information to localize the projection of the point P on the ground plane, which we denote with G. Once we know the image location of the projection of the 3D point P to the ground, G, we can project this point to the world-coordinate axis.

motivation.text: In the absence of any other information, we can not recover the 3D location of a single point P from a single view. But real world scenes are composed by a multitude of objects providing context, which allows solving the 3D estimation problem even with just a single image.

concepts.title: Camera Calibration from Vanishing Points
concepts.one_liner: Camera intrinsics can be estimated from three orthogonal vanishing points by solving for the conic matrix under the constraint of 3D orthogonality.
concepts.content:
Camera parameters can be extracted using only vanishing points, provided certain conditions are met. In scenes with many parallel lines aligned with the world coordinate system, the three vanishing points $\mathbf{v}_i$ correspond to three orthogonal 3D directions $\mathbf{D}_i$. The relationship between these is given by $\mathbf{D}_i = \mathbf{R}^{-1} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{v}_i$. Because the directions are orthogonal ($\mathbf{D}_i^{\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{D}_j = 0$), we derive a constraint that depends only on the intrinsic parameters $\mathbf{K}$:
$$\mathbf{v}_i^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{K}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{v}_j = 0$$
We define the conic matrix $\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{K}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{K}^{-1}$. Assuming the camera skew is zero, $\mathbf{W}$ has a specific structure with four unknown values. These values can be solved as a system of linear equations $\mathbf{A} \mathbf{w} = 0$ using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). Finally, $\mathbf{K}$ is recovered from $\mathbf{W}$ via Cholesky factorization and normalization.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional camera calibration requires specialized patterns or known 3D point correspondences. This method allows for 'self-calibration' using only the geometric structure (parallel and orthogonal lines) naturally present in man-made environments like offices or city streets.
concepts.recap_md: - Orthogonal vanishing points provide linear constraints on the camera's intrinsic matrix.

key_passage.text: We will use the vanishing points to derive a set of constraints on the projection matrix. To do this, we start by inverting equation: $\mathbf{D}_i = \mathbf{R}^{-1} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{v}_i$ Because the vectors $\mathbf{D}_i$ are orthogonal, we have that $\mathbf{D}_i^{\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{D}_j = 0$ for $i \neq j$.

concepts.title: Single View Metrology
concepts.one_liner: Single view metrology recovers three-dimensional information about a scene from a single two-dimensional image by understanding the geometry of image formation and perspective rules.
concepts.content: The goal of single view metrology is to recover three-dimensional (3D) information about a scene from a single image. (see figure: Is it possible to recover three-dimensional (3D) scene information from a single two-dimensional (2D) image? How tall is the desk? How wide is the bookshelf? What do we need to know about the scene...) This approach relies on understanding the geometry of the image formation process, the rules of perspective, and other visual cues present in the image. Unlike methods such as stereo vision, structure from motion, or multiview geometry, which utilize multiple images, single view metrology derives cues for 3D estimation from first principles using a single viewpoint. This is particularly important for applications where only one view is available, such as analyzing paintings or photographs, or when stereo vision is ineffective due to small disparity at large distances.
concepts.motivation_md: It is often necessary to estimate 3D structure when only a single image is available, such as in historical photographs or paintings. Additionally, stereo vision fails at long distances where disparity is negligible, making single-view geometric cues essential.
concepts.recap_md: - Single view metrology recovers 3D scene information from a single 2D image using perspective cues.

concepts.title: Ames Room

position.section_title: A Few Notes about Perception of Depth by Humans

concepts.one_liner: The Ames room is an irregular room that appears perfectly rectangular from a specific vantage point, creating a powerful 3D visual illusion of changing object sizes.
concepts.content: The Ames room is an irregular room constructed so that when viewed with one eye from a particular vantage point, the room appears to be perfectly rectangular. This is achieved by making the part of the wall that is farther away from the viewer larger so that it appears fronto-parallel. [FIGURE:4b865b0ab7d9d5dd] When looking through the designated aperture on the wall, the room appears square and smaller than it actually is. (see figure: Make your own Ames room. Take a picture of this page and print it as large as you can (A4 or letter size will be sufficient). When you look through the aperture on the *front wall*, the room will...) This illusion is especially remarkable when the room is large enough for people to walk in; as people walk along the back wall, they appear to change in height because the brain disregards prior expectations about size in favor of the perceived rectangular geometry. [FIGURE:db734c72cbd8a0cd] [FIGURE:845b1e8c4509a400] If an object is placed along the back wall, its perceived size changes, and doors of different real sizes may appear identical.
concepts.motivation_md: The Ames room demonstrates how the human visual system relies on geometric priors, like the assumption that rooms are rectangular, which can be exploited to create powerful size illusions.
concepts.recap_md: - The Ames room is a non-rectangular space designed to appear rectangular from a specific viewpoint.

key_passage.text: The Ames room is an irregular room constructed in such a way that when you look at it with one eye from a particular vantage point, the room appears to be perfectly rectangular. This is achieved by making the part of the wall that is farther away from the viewer larger so that it appears fronto-parallel.

motivation.text: 3D visual illusions are remarkably powerful. One captivating 3D illusion is the Ames room.

concepts.title: Linear Perspective
concepts.one_liner: Linear perspective uses parallel lines, vanishing points, and the horizon line to infer 3D scene structure from a 2D image.
concepts.content: Linear perspective uses parallel and orthogonal lines, vanishing points, the ground plane, and the horizon line to infer the 3D scene structure from a 2D image. Attributed to the Italian architect Filippo Brunelleschi in 1415, linear perspective relies on a few assumptions about the scene. Consequently, it is not a general cue useful in all scenes, but it is very powerful in most human-made environments.
concepts.motivation_md: Linear perspective provides a mathematical framework for representing 3D depth on a 2D surface, which is essential for both realistic art and computer vision in man-made environments.
concepts.recap_md: - It utilizes geometric features like vanishing points and horizon lines to reconstruct 3D structure.

concepts.title: Projection of 3D Lines
concepts.one_liner: In perspective projection, 3D lines are projected into 2D lines on the camera plane based on their parametric vector form.
concepts.content: In perspective projection, 3D lines project into 2D lines in the camera plane. A 3D line can be parameterized using a point $\mathbf{P}_0=[X_0, Y_0, Z_0]^\mathsf{T}$ and a direction vector $\mathbf{D} = [D_X, D_Y, D_Z]^\mathsf{T}$ as: $$\mathbf{P}_t = \begin{bmatrix} X_0 + t D_x\\ Y_0 + t D_y\\ Z_0 + t D_z \end{bmatrix}$$ (see figure: Projection of a 3D line onto the camera plane. The 3D line and the camera center form a plane (the camera center is a the world-coordinates origin). The intersection of this plane with the camera...) The equation of the resulting 2D line in the image plane is obtained using perspective projection equations: $$\mathbf{p}_t = \begin{bmatrix} x_t\\ y_t \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} f \dfrac{ X_0 + t D_X}{Z_0 + t D_Z}\\[12pt] f \dfrac{ Y_0 + t D_Y}{Z_0 + t D_Z} \end{bmatrix}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding how 3D lines map to 2D image coordinates is the fundamental step in modeling how cameras capture the world and how we can reverse that process.
concepts.recap_md: - 3D lines are represented parametrically using a starting point and a direction vector.

concepts.title: Vanishing Point
concepts.one_liner: A vanishing point is the finite point in a 2D image where the projections of parallel 3D lines converge as they extend to infinity.
concepts.content: Even though a line in 3D space extends infinitely, its 2D projection converges to a finite point called the vanishing point in the limit as $t$ goes to infinity: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{v} = \lim_{t \to \infty} \mathbf{p}_t = \left [ \begin{array}{c} f \dfrac{D_X}{D_Z}\\[12pt] f \dfrac{D_Y}{D_Z} \end{array} \right ]\end{aligned}$$ The vanishing point $\mathbf{v} = [v_x, v_y]^\mathsf{T}$ depends only on the direction vector $\mathbf{D}$. Consequently, all parallel lines in 3D project into non-parallel 2D images that converge to the same vanishing point in the image. If $D_Z = 0$, the 3D line is parallel to the camera plane and the vanishing point is at infinity. (see figure: Parallel 3D lines converge to the same vanishing point. (a) The red lines are parallel to the optical axis and converge to a vanishing point in the center. (b) Two sets of parallel lines contained in...)
concepts.motivation_md: Vanishing points allow us to determine the 3D orientation of lines from a single image, as the point of convergence depends solely on the direction of the parallel lines.
concepts.recap_md: - Parallel 3D lines converge to a single vanishing point in the 2D image plane.

concepts.title: Horizon Line
concepts.one_liner: The horizon line is the line in an image that contains the vanishing points of all lines within a specific 3D plane.
concepts.content: Any 3D plane becomes a half-plane in the image and has a horizon line. The horizon line is the line that passes through all the vanishing points of all the lines contained in the plane. (see figure: All parallel lines contained in a plane converge to a set of vanishing points. All those vanishing points are contained in the **horizon line** of the plane. Parallel planes have the same horizon...) Parallel planes share the same horizon line. The ground plane is a special plane because the point of contact between objects and the ground informs about distance; objects further away have a contact point projecting onto a higher point in the image plane relative to the horizon. The horizon line can be detected using homogeneous coordinates: the intersection of two projected parallel lines (computed via cross-product $\boldsymbol{l}_1 \times \boldsymbol{l}_2$) gives a vanishing point, and the line passing through two such vanishing points from the same plane is the horizon line. (see figure: Using parallel lines, in homogeneous coordinates, to compute vanishing points and the horizon line.)
concepts.motivation_md: The horizon line provides a reference for the orientation of planes and helps estimate the relative distance of objects based on their contact point with the ground.
concepts.recap_md: - The horizon line is formed by the set of all vanishing points for lines within a 3D plane.

concepts.title: Detecting Vanishing Points
concepts.one_liner: Vanishing points can be detected manually by intersecting parallel edges or automatically using edge detection, RANSAC, or deep learning models.
concepts.content: Vanishing points can be estimated manually by selecting pairs of long edges in an image corresponding to parallel 3D lines in the scene and finding their intersection. (see figure: Most object boundaries in this photograph are oriented parallel to one of the world-coordinates reference frame (the world-coordinates frame is chosen in this way on purpose). All the parallel 3D...) Automatically, vanishing points are extracted by first detecting image edges and orientations and then using RANSAC to group the edges: every pair of edges votes for a vanishing point, and the point with the largest support is selected. Modern learning-based approaches also exist, utilizing graphical models or deep learning architectures such as DeepVP and NeurVPS.
concepts.motivation_md: Automating the detection of vanishing points is crucial for robotic navigation and automated 3D reconstruction from standard photographs.
concepts.recap_md: - Vanishing points are found by intersecting the 2D projections of parallel 3D lines.

key_passage.text: Vanishing points can be extracted automatically from images by first detecting image edges and their orientations and then using RANSAC to group the edges: every pair of edges will vote for a vanishing point and the point with the largest support will be considered a vanishing point.

concepts.title: Cross-Ratio
concepts.one_liner: The cross-ratio is a projective invariant of four collinear points that remains constant under perspective projection.
concepts.content: While perspective projection changes angles and relative lengths, the cross-ratio of four collinear points is a geometric property that is preserved. It is defined by the expression: $$CR \left( \mathbf{P}_1,\mathbf{P}_2,\mathbf{P}_3,\mathbf{P}_4 \right) = \frac{\left| \mathbf{P}_3 -\mathbf{P}_1 \right| \left|\mathbf{P}_4 -\mathbf{P}_2 \right|} {\left| \mathbf{P}_3 -\mathbf{P}_2 \right| \left|\mathbf{P}_4 -\mathbf{P}_1 \right|}$$ where $\left| \mathbf{P}_i -\mathbf{P}_j \right|$ is the Euclidean distance between points. [FIGURE:c3a83d33f5a7a7b5] Two sets of points $\mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{Q}$ related by a projective transformation have the same cross-ratio: $CR(\mathbf{P}_1,\mathbf{P}_2,\mathbf{P}_3,\mathbf{P}_4) = CR(\mathbf{Q}_1,\mathbf{Q}_2,\mathbf{Q}_3,\mathbf{Q}_4)$. (see figure: The set of points $\mathbf{P}$ are related to the points $\mathbf{Q}$ (and $\mathbf{R}$) by the cross-ratio. The point $\mathbf{R}_1$ is in infinity because the line connecting the points...) The order of points matters; there are 24 possible orderings resulting in six different values. When one point is at infinity, the terms containing that point cancel out, simplifying the cross-ratio to a ratio of distances: $CR(\mathbf{R}_1,\mathbf{R}_2,\mathbf{R}_3,\mathbf{R}_4) = \frac{\left| \mathbf{R}_4 -\mathbf{R}_2 \right| } { \left| \mathbf{R}_3 -\mathbf{R}_2 \right|}$.
concepts.motivation_md: The cross-ratio is a fundamental tool in metrology because it allows for the calculation of real-world distances from images without knowing the camera's internal parameters.
concepts.recap_md: - The cross-ratio is a projective invariant, meaning it stays constant even after perspective projection.

key_passage.text: The cross-ratio of four collinear points is defined by the expression: CR(P1,P2,P3,P4) = |P3-P1||P4-P2| / |P3-P2||P4-P1| where |Pi-Pj| is the euclidean distance between points Pi and Pj, using heterogeneous coordinates. The cross-ratio is considered the most important projective invariant.

motivation.text: Fortunately, some geometric properties are preserved under perspective projection. For instance, straight lines remain straight. Are there other quantities that are preserved? The cross-ratio is one of those quantities.
